title: Why Does My Refinished Floor Look Blotchy? 7 Contractor Mistakes to Avoid in Lynnwood
meta: A blotchy refinished floor usually means skipped grits, uneven water-popping or stain wiped unevenly. Wills Flooring lists 7 contractor mistakes in Lynnwood.
keywords: refinished hardwood floor looks blotchy, why is my stained floor blotchy, uneven stain on hardwood floors, hardwood refinishing mistakes, floor refinishing Lynnwood WA

blocks.lead: A blotchy refinished floor almost always comes from the sanding and staining steps, not the finish: skipped grits, an uneven water-pop, stain left on too long in some spots and wiped hard in others, or an edger that cut deeper than the drum.
blocks.detail: Most of them cannot be fixed with another coat. The real fix is sanding back to bare wood and doing it right: $3.99 per sq ft natural or $6.50 with stain at Wills Flooring, 500 sq ft minimum. Here are the seven mistakes we see most in Lynnwood and how to spot each.

blocks.html: We get a version of this call every month from Lynnwood: the carpet came up in an Alderwood or Martha Lake rambler, the oak got sanded and stained, and now there are dark patches by the walls, lighter lanes down the middle and a cloudy zone by the slider. Is it the wood or the work? Sometimes the wood. Usually the work. This is the checklist we use to tell the difference, and it tells you whether a screen and recoat can save the floor or whether it has to be sanded again.

blocks.text: The 7 contractor mistakes behind a blotchy floor

items.title: Skipped sanding grits
items.text: Jumping from 36 grit to 100 leaves deep scratches under the fine ones. Stain floods those scratches and the floor looks darker in lanes. Look for straight dark streaks in the direction the drum ran.

items.title: Edger cut deeper than the drum
items.text: The edger spins a disc; the drum runs with the grain. When the two are not blended with a final orbital pass, a 6 to 8 inch dark band appears around every wall. This is picture framing, the most common Lynnwood complaint.

items.title: Uneven or skipped water-pop
items.text: Wetting the sanded floor opens the grain so stain takes evenly. Popping one area heavily and another lightly gives you dark clouds next to pale patches with soft edges.

items.title: Stain wiped inconsistently
items.text: Stain that sits five minutes in one area and one minute in another will not match, and neither will a fresh rag next to a saturated one. The tell is blotches shaped like rag strokes or hard edges where sections met.

items.title: Finish applied before stain dried
items.text: Water-based finish over damp oil stain lifts and smears it. You get milky patches and a soft finish that dents easily. Common when a crew tries to fit stain and coats into one day.

items.title: Dust and contamination
items.text: Sanding dust, dog hair or silicone from furniture polish left on the floor before the coat produces fisheyes, specks and dull spots. Not a color problem, but it reads as blotchy in low-angle light.

items.title: Sanding in bad light
items.text: Buffer swirls, drum stop marks and missed edger passes are invisible under an overhead light and obvious under a window. A crew that never checks with a raking light misses all of it.

blocks.text: Price a proper re-sand in Lynnwood right now

blocks.note: A blotchy stained floor needs the stain option to come back the same color. A blotchy natural floor may only need the natural rate. Dust containment is worth it if you are living in the house.

blocks.text: Can a screen and recoat fix it?

a.title: When the problem is in the finish
items: Dull or streaky sheen from a bad final coat
Fisheyes and dust specks in the topcoat
The color underneath is even and you are happy with it

b.title: When the problem is in the wood or stain
items: Sanding scratches you can feel with a fingernail
Any problem that shows through a clear coat today; it will show through another one

blocks.text: How a re-sand is done right

items.text: Drum sander through 36, 60, 80 and 100 grit, edger through the same sequence, then a hand scrape in the corners. Nothing skipped.
An orbital pass blends the edger zone into the field. Every room is checked with a light held at floor level from three sides.
The whole floor is wetted evenly, allowed to dry fully, then stained in sections with a fixed dwell time and clean rags. One person applies, one wipes, so the rhythm never changes.
Stain dries overnight, longer in a damp Lynnwood winter. We do not coat a stained floor the same day.
Three coats of Bona water-based finish, abraded between coats, with the room sealed against dust.
items.note: Example: 780 sq ft Meadowdale rambler × $6.50 + $250 containment = $5,320

blocks.text: Mistakes homeowners make after a bad job

items.html: Not calling the original contractor first. If the crew is licensed and offers a warranty, a blotchy stain job is on them. Document it in daylight, in writing, before anyone touches it.
Accepting a free recoat as the remedy. If the blotch is in the stain, a recoat locks it in and adds to what has to come off later.
Forgetting the wood is thinner now. Every sanding removes wood. Before a re-sand, ask how much is left above the tongue. Most Lynnwood oak has plenty; a floor done three times before may not.
Hiring the next crew on price alone. Look for a Bona Certified Craftsman and a written workmanship warranty this time.

blocks.text: How to make sure it does not happen again

items: Ask what grit sequence the crew uses and how they blend the edger into the field. A real answer names grits and a buffer.
Ask whether they water-pop before stain, and whether stain and finish happen on different days.
Ask for a stain test on your actual floor, in a closet, before the whole house.
Walk the sanded floor with a flashlight at floor level before stain goes down. Anything you see then, you will see forever.
Ask about dust containment. The $250 option seals the rooms and runs an air scrubber, which also protects the coats from contamination.

Get the square footage, grit sequence, stain and number of coats in writing, backed by a workmanship warranty. Ours at Wills Flooring is one year, done by a Bona Certified Craftsman, minutes from our Lynnwood showroom on 196th.

faq.q: Why does my refinished floor look blotchy after staining?
faq.a: The usual reasons are an uneven water-pop before stain, stain left on for different lengths of time across the room, skipped sanding grits, and an edger that cut deeper along the walls than the drum did in the middle. All four are workmanship issues and show as clouds, lanes or a dark border.

faq.q: Can a blotchy stained floor be fixed without sanding again?
faq.a: Rarely. Stain lives in the wood, so a screen and recoat, which only abrades the finish, leaves the blotches in place under a new coat. If the color is even and only the sheen is streaky or dusty, a recoat at $1.99 per sq ft works. Otherwise the floor has to be re-sanded.

faq.q: How much does it cost to fix a blotchy refinished floor in Lynnwood?
faq.a: A full re-sand at Wills Flooring is $3.99 per sq ft for a natural finish or $6.50 with stain, 500 sq ft minimum. A 780 sq ft rambler re-stained with dust containment comes to $5,320. If the original contractor is licensed and warranties their work, they should cover it.

faq.q: What is picture framing on a hardwood floor?
faq.a: A darker band, usually 6 to 8 inches wide, along every wall. It happens when the edger sands the perimeter to a different depth or scratch pattern than the drum used in the middle, and the two are not blended before stain. A recoat will not fix it.

faq.q: Do some woods stain blotchy no matter what?
faq.a: Yes. Maple, birch, fir and pine have tight or uneven grain that absorbs stain irregularly. A good contractor says so up front and uses a conditioner, water-pops carefully, chooses a lighter color or recommends a natural finish. Red oak, the usual Lynnwood floor, stains evenly.

faq.q: Should I let the original contractor try to fix it?
faq.a: If they are licensed, insured and offer a warranty, give them the first chance and put your complaint in writing with daylight photos. Ask specifically for a re-sand, not a recoat. If they refuse or want to charge you again, get a second opinion before more finish goes down.
